title: High-quality single crystals of the kagome metals Ni$_3$In and Ni$_3$Sn grown from Pb flux
authors: Fabian Garmroudi, Jennifer Coulter, Caitlin S. T. Kengle, Joe D. Thompson, Eric D. Bauer, Sean M. Thomas, Priscila F. S. Rosa
abstract: The bilayer kagome metal Ni$_3$In has recently attracted attention due to the presence of a flat band located near the Fermi level, which has been associated with unconventional thermodynamic and electronic transport properties [Ye et al., Nat. Phys. 20, 610-614 (2024)]. However, further investigation of the intrinsic properties of this system has been hindered by the lack of large, high-quality single crystals. Here, we report the successful growth of Ni$_3$(In, Sn) single crystals using a Pb-flux technique. By optimizing the growth conditions, competing binary phases can be effectively suppressed, enabling the synthesis of single crystals with dimensions reaching several millimeters. We compare the physical properties of our Pb-flux-grown crystals to previously reported samples prepared by iodine-assisted chemical vapor transport and molecular beam epitaxy as well as to first-principles resistivity calculations. We find a significantly lower electrical resistivity in our crystals, in excellent agreement with calculations of resistivity from electron-phonon scattering, a sizeable non-saturating magnetoresistance, and a reduced Sommerfeld coefficient and magnetic susceptibility compared to previous experimental findings, which are likely related to differences in the Fermi level position. Our results establish Pb-flux growth as a reliable route for obtaining large single crystals of the bilayer kagome metals Ni$_3$(In, Sn) that are suitable for further thermodynamic and spectroscopic investigations of their intrinsic electronic and magnetic properties.
summary: This work successfully develops a reliable Pb-flux method for growing large single crystals of kagome metals Ni3In and Ni3Sn. By characterizing these new samples, the authors find improved electronic quality compared to prior reports, revealing signatures of correlated electron behavior through measurements like specific heat and magnetoresistance.
main_problem: The intrinsic electronic and magnetic properties of kagome metals like Ni3In are difficult to study due to the lack of large, high-quality single crystals.
main_result: Growing these materials using a Pb-flux technique yields significantly higher quality crystals compared to previous methods, leading to measurements that suggest correlated electron behavior deviating from simple band theory predictions.
method: The authors report crystal growth via the Pb-flux method and characterize the resulting samples using transport (resistivity, magnetoresistance) and thermodynamic (specific heat, susceptibility) measurements, comparing them against DFT calculations.
model_or_system: The study focuses on bilayer kagome metals Ni3In and Ni3Sn, which are characterized by flat bands near the Fermi level. The electronic structure is modeled using Density Functional Theory (DFT), and transport properties are calculated using Boltzmann theory approximations.
key_observables: Electrical resistivity ($ho$), magnetoresistance (MR), Sommerfeld coefficient ($\gamma$), magnetic susceptibility ($\chi(T)$), and Kadowaki-Woods ratio ($A/\gamma^2$).
important_parameters: Low temperatures ($<1.5 	ext{ K}$), Fermi level position relative to flat bands, and the flux growth temperature/composition.
main_assumptions: The comparison between measured $\gamma$ and DFT predictions suggests correlated electron behavior, but a simple rigid-band shift of $E_F$ cannot account for the discrepancy.
figures_summary: Figures compare crystal structures (hexagonal), Density of States showing flat bands, and temperature dependencies of magnetic susceptibility ($\chi(T)$) and specific heat ($C/T$) between flux-grown and previously synthesized samples.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the necessity of high-quality crystals via Pb-flux growth. It then compares physical measurements (resistivity, MR, $\gamma$, $\chi$) from these new crystals against prior work and theoretical calculations to deduce intrinsic electronic properties.
why_interesting: While focused on solid-state materials, the investigation into flat bands and anomalous transport coefficients ($\gamma$ vs. DFT) touches upon strongly correlated electron physics, which shares conceptual links with many-body dynamics studied in AMO physics.
